content: Laboratory protocols for serological testing of HCV antibodies were conducted using the Cobas 8000 platform (Roche Molecular Systems, USA). This system utilized single-use disposable tips to ensure precision and minimize contamination risks. Reflex HCV RNA testing was performed on a second, unopened specimen using flow cytometry. The quantification of HCV RNA was carried out using the Cobas 6800 analyzer (Roche Molecular Systems, USA). Prior to HCV RNA determination, blood count analysis was conducted using a Sysmex XN-20 analyzer (Sysmex Corporation, Japan), which allowed hematimetric measurements without the need to uncap blood tubes, as the rubber cap was punctured by a needle. The Vall d’Hebron laboratory decided against using a single specimen for both serological and virologic testing due to the high risk of cross-contamination. The Cobas 6800 analyzer, used for serological testing, centralizes serological determinations and tends to concentrate specimens with serological evidence of HCV infection (e.g., anti-HCV positive). Despite the use of disposable tips in the Cobas 8000 analyzer, specimens are uncapped during analysis, making them susceptible to environmental aerosols and manual handling, which increases contamination risks. Consequently, the laboratory mandated that serological specimens should not be used for virologic determinations. In contrast, blood count determinations are processed randomly, with over 5,000 samples analyzed daily. This random distribution statistically reduces the likelihood of cross-contamination between anti-HCV-positive cases (approximately 5–10 per day) and minimizes the risk of a positive HCV RNA specimen contaminating a nearby negative sample. No formal economic analysis has been conducted to compare the cost of HCV reflex testing in the Vall d’Hebron laboratory network with conventional two-step testing strategies. However, laboratory representatives noted that the cost of viral RNA determination (less than €30) is significantly lower than the cost of a second physician appointment and blood collection. The British Columbia Centre for Disease Control Public Health Laboratory (BCCDC PHL) serves as the primary public health and reference diagnostic testing facility for British Columbia, Canada. By the end of 2019, analyses of the BC Hepatitis Testers Cohort revealed that approximately 16% of individuals in BC who tested HCV antibody-positive had never undergone HCV RNA NAT testing. To address this gap, automated HCV RNA NAT reflex testing was proposed to improve the assessment of active HCV infection following positive screening results. This approach aimed to enhance the HCV care cascade by reducing patient visits, minimizing blood collections, and potentially alleviating physicians’ workloads. Reflex testing was introduced in January 2020, requiring the development of laboratory standard operating procedures, process mapping, and staff training. No capital investments were necessary. Four main challenges were addressed: validating serum specimens for HCV RNA NAT assays, revising laboratory workflows and information systems, training staff and developing job aids, and educating clinicians about the reflex testing pathway. In clinical settings, all in-patient and out-patient facilities within the laboratory network are eligible for reflex testing. HCV RNA NAT results from reflex tests are reported separately from initial anti-HCV results but are accessible in the patient’s electronic testing record. The typical turnaround time for test results is five days. Serum specimens are stored at 4°C before anti-HCV screening on the Siemens Centaur XP System analyzer. If supplemental testing confirms anti-HCV positivity with a screen index value >11, the patient’s previous HCV testing history is reviewed. If the patient is newly anti-HCV positive or has never undergone HCV RNA NAT testing, the reflex test is accessioned, and the specimen is sent for HCV RNA NAT testing using Abbott m2000 or Abbott Alinity platforms. If an EDTA plasma specimen is available, it is preferentially used for HCV NAT; otherwise, the original serum specimen is utilized. If serum is used and HCV RNA is not detected, a follow-up EDTA blood HCV RNA test is requested to minimize the risk of false-negative results due to serum integrity concerns. Samples for virologic testing are stored for up to 14 days, and any remaining positive specimens are aliquoted and stored indefinitely at −20°C. In England, the 2012 UK Public Health Guidelines recommended automatic HCV RNA testing for anti-HCV-positive specimens or referral to a laboratory capable of performing this test. However, due to the higher cost of RNA testing compared to anti-HCV testing, automatic RNA testing was not widely implemented unless specifically requested. A 2013 study by Public Health England found that only 53% of anti-HCV-positive specimens underwent routine HCV RNA NAT testing before reflex testing recommendations were introduced.
